c.tagline: Highland capital where colonial plazas meet Central America's liveliest urban scene.

taxi.fareNote: Meters are uncommon; agree on the fare (or use an app-based rideshare) before starting the ride.

emergency.medical: 125 Cruz Roja (ambulance) / 123 Bomberos Municipales / 122 Bomberos Voluntarios

hood_landmark.Zona 1 (Centro Histórico): Plaza de la Constitución, Guatemala City

avoid.reason: Avoid Zones 1, 3, 6, 18 and 21 — high crime; stay in Zonas 10/14 (Zona Viva); use registered taxis

hood_desc: The city's upscale hub of hotels, embassies, restaurants, and nightlife around Plaza Fontabella; best for business travelers and visitors who want comfort and walkable dining close to the action.

Colonial-era Centro Histórico with the National Palace, cathedral, and Plaza Mayor; suits history buffs and budget travelers comfortable with a lively, gritty downtown that empties out and feels less safe after dark.
A leafy, quiet zone by the airport with the city's best museums and La Aurora Zoo; ideal for travelers with early flights, families, or anyone wanting easy airport access away from the bustle.
Guatemala City's arts and nightlife district, Cuatro Grados Norte, packed with converted-factory bars, street art, and design shops; suits younger travelers and culture seekers.
A calmer business district bordering Zona Viva, anchored by the Torre del Reformador; good for business travelers wanting Zona 10 proximity at somewhat lower prices.

water.note: Avoid tap water; stick to bottled or purified water.

transit.pay: Transmetro and Transurbano use a rechargeable prepaid "Tarjeta Ciudadana" card (cash is no longer accepted on Transmetro); regular municipal buses ("camionetas"/red buses) take small-denomination quetzal cash paid to the driver.
transit.hours: Transmetro/Transurbano run roughly 5am-9/10pm daily; there is no late-night rail or metro service, so taxis or rideshare apps are the norm after dark.
transit.note: Standard citywide "red buses" have a history of safety incidents in some areas; Transmetro BRT, registered taxis, and rideshare apps are the options recommended to visitors.

bus: Intercity coaches: Litegua, Rutas Orientales, Hedman Alas, ADN

airport.name: La Aurora International Airport (GUA)
airport.drive: 15-25 min to Zona 10 (longer in rush-hour traffic)

transit.m: Local city bus (Ruta) to nearest terminal, ~10 min walk from terminal, not recommended with luggage

tip.r: A 10% tip (propina) is appreciated at restaurants but not obligatory - some upscale places already add a service charge, so check the bill. Rounding up is common for taxis; small cash tips for hotel porters/housekeeping are customary.

food.name: Pepian
food.desc: Guatemala's national stew and a pre-Hispanic survivor: chicken or beef in a dark sauce of toasted pumpkin and sesame seeds, chillies and tomato.

places.name: Kacao
places.note: Thatched-roof landmark of traditional Guatemalan cooking; the standard tourist-friendly pepian.

places.name: Arrin Cuan
places.note: Decades-old Coban-rooted kitchen with marimba music and a heavily local crowd.

places.name: Restaurante El Adobe
places.note: Known for authentic pepian served with live marimba in the historic centre.

food.name: Kak'ik
food.desc: Q'eqchi' Maya turkey soup from Alta Verapaz, deep red with achiote and cobanero chilli, served with tamalitos and rice. Officially protected heritage.

places.name: Arrin Cuan
places.note: Coban specialities are the house's reason for being; the most reliable kak'ik in town.

places.name: Kacao
places.note: Serves kak'ik alongside the full roster of regional Maya dishes.

places.name: 7 Caldos
places.note: Soup house built around traditional broths, kak'ik and jocon included.

food.name: Chuchitos
food.desc: Small firm corn-dough tamales tied in a husk, stuffed with pork or chicken and recado sauce. Sold from baskets and steamers all day long.

places.name: Mercado Central
places.note: Comedor stalls under the cathedral steam chuchitos and tamales from the morning on.

places.name: La Cocina de la Senora Pu
places.note: Tiny Maya kitchen doing careful versions of home dishes; book, it is very small.

places.name: Arrin Cuan
places.note: Chuchitos and tamales as starters if you would rather sit down than eat standing.

food.name: Tostadas
food.desc: Crisp fried tortillas topped with guacamol, black bean paste or cooked tomato salsa, dusted with parsley and cheese. The classic street snack.

places.name: Mercado Central
places.note: Rows of stands building tostadas to order for a couple of quetzales each.

places.name: Sexta Avenida
places.note: Pedestrian avenue where evening carts sell tostadas, atol and elote loco.

places.name: Kacao
places.note: Sit-down tostada platter if you want them in a restaurant setting.

food.name: Jocon
food.desc: Chicken stewed in a bright green sauce of tomatillo, coriander and spring onion thickened with toasted seeds; one of the four great recados.

places.name: 7 Caldos
places.note: The pollo en jocon is the dish regulars order here; generous and inexpensive.

places.name: Arrin Cuan
places.note: Traditional jocon on a menu of highland classics, marimba most evenings.

places.name: Kacao
places.note: Reliable jocon in a comfortable room; good for a first taste of the recados.

food.name: Tamales and paches
food.desc: Weekend and holiday food: soft corn tamales wrapped in banana leaf, and paches made with potato dough. Traditionally eaten on Saturday night.

places.name: Mercado Central
places.note: Steamer baskets of tamales colorados and paches, best on Saturdays.

places.name: Arrin Cuan
places.note: Serves tamales year round rather than only at weekends.

places.name: La Cocina de la Senora Pu
places.note: Hand-made versions using traditional recados and leaf wrapping.

food.name: Guatemalan coffee
food.desc: Antigua, Huehuetenango and Coban beans are world class, and the capital's specialty cafes finally keep the good lots at home instead of exporting them.

places.name: Cafe Leon
places.note: Historic roaster and cafe in the old centre, a fixture of downtown coffee drinking.

places.name: Fat Cat Coffee House
places.note: Specialty roaster with single-origin Guatemalan lots and pour-over service.

places.name: Mercado Central
places.note: Bags of regional beans sold cheaply straight from the producing regions.

food.name: Atol de elote
food.desc: Hot sweet corn drink thickened almost to a porridge, sold from steaming pots at dusk. Its cousins are atol blanco and cinnamon-scented arroz en leche.

places.name: Sexta Avenida
places.note: Evening atol carts set up along the pedestrian street; cups cost a few quetzales.

places.name: Mercado Central
places.note: Atol and horchata poured all day at the comedor counters.

places.name: Kacao
places.note: Atol and traditional cacao drinks on the menu in a sit-down setting.

landmarks: Metropolitan Cathedral
This grand neoclassical cathedral facing Central Park has anchored Guatemala City's historic center since the 1800s, its facade inscribed with the names of civil war victims.
National Palace of Culture
A sprawling green sandstone palace of murals, stained glass, and courtyards, this former seat of government is now a museum showcasing Guatemala's political and artistic history.
Central Park (Parque Central)
The bustling civic heart of the capital, this plaza is framed by the cathedral and national palace and comes alive with vendors, marimba music, and photographers.
Reformer's Tower (Torre del Reformador)
This Eiffel Tower-inspired iron structure honors 19th-century reformist president Justo Rufino Barrios and remains a beloved skyline landmark, especially striking when lit at night.
Relief Map (Mapa en Relieve)
An enormous 1905 topographic model depicting Guatemala's mountains, rivers, and coastlines to scale, offering visitors a fascinating bird's-eye view of the whole country.
Miguel Ángel Asturias Cultural Center
Home to the National Theater's striking sail-like white architecture perched on a hilltop, this venue is a modernist icon and hub of Guatemalan performing arts.
Kaminaljuyu Archaeological Site
Grass-covered Maya pyramid mounds tucked within the modern city offer a rare glimpse into a pre-Columbian metropolis that once rivaled the greatest Mesoamerican centers.
San Francisco Church
A richly baroque colonial church renowned for its ornate carved altar and the tomb of beloved friar Hermano Pedro, drawing pilgrims and architecture lovers alike.
Cerro del Carmen
A hillside chapel and lookout point offering sweeping panoramic views over the capital's rooftops and surrounding volcanoes, popular at sunset with locals and visitors.
Mercado Central
A multi-level indoor market packed with colorful textiles, handicrafts, and local food stalls, offering an immersive taste of everyday Guatemalan culture and commerce.

train.note: Guatemala has no passenger railway - the old FEGUA network is long defunct and a planned Guatemala City light-rail ('Metro Riel') is not yet running. Travel is by intercity coach or car.

intl.to: San Salvador, Tegucigalpa, Managua, San José & Panama City (+ Tapachula, Mexico)

bus.note: Tica Bus is the main cross-border coach, linking Guatemala City to every Central American capital and to Tapachula in Mexico; buses leave from its Zona 13 terminal. Carry your passport for the border stops.

ferry.note: Guatemala City is inland, so no ferries run from the capital. Guatemala's only notable passenger boats are far away on the Caribbean coast (Río Dulce and Lívingston), and there is no scheduled international passenger ferry.

half.name: Antigua Guatemala
half.blurb: A UNESCO colonial city of cobbled streets, baroque ruins and volcano views.

half.name: Pacaya Volcano
half.blurb: An active volcano with lava fields and hikes across steaming black terrain.

half.name: Iximché
half.blurb: Grassy pre-Columbian ruins that once served as the Kaqchikel Maya capital.

full.name: Lake Atitlán
full.blurb: A stunning volcano-ringed lake dotted with traditional Maya villages along its shores.

full.name: Chichicastenango
full.blurb: Home to one of Central America's largest and most colorful indigenous markets.
